result.markdown: --- title: "[Graph.has_node()]{.doc-object-name .doc-function .doc-label .doc-label-method}" body-classes: doc-api-page doc-py-api-page shift-heading-level-by: 0 toc-depth: 3 page-navigation: false html-table-processing: none --- ::: {.doc-subject} Check if a node exists in the graph. ::: ::: {.doc-usage-source} Usage [Source](https://github.com/rich-iannone/edgecase/blob/main/python/edgecase/graph.py#L14867-L14949){target="_blank" rel="noopener"} ::: ::: {.doc-signature .doc-Kind.FUNCTION} ```python Graph.has_node(node) ``` ::: ::: {.doc-text} ![Has node](/assets/graphs/has-node.light.svg){.lightbox fig-alt="Left: the shared four-node graph queried for C, which is outlined in the accent color; has_node returns True. Right: the same graph queried for E, drawn as a dashed outline where it would be; there is no such node, so has_node returns False." width="100%"} Verifies whether a node, given either by its integer ID or by its string label, is present in the graph. An integer is always treated as a node ID and a string is always treated as a label, so `has_node(3)` and `has_node("3")` ask different questions: the first looks for node ID `3`, the second for a node labelled `"3"`. Unlike most methods that accept a node, `has_node()` doesn't raise when the label or ID isn't in the graph; it simply returns `False`. That makes it a safe guard to use: - before calling methods that raise on a missing node (e.g. `neighbors()`, `delete_node()`) - when deciding whether to add a node or update an existing one while loading data - when validating user-supplied identifiers The check is against the whole graph and is not affected by the current selection. ::: ## Parameters {.doc-parameters} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [node]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [Union[int, str]]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : The node to look for: an `int` is matched against node IDs and a `str` is matched against node labels. Values of any other type (e.g. a `float` like `1.0`, or a `bool`) are not valid identifiers and make the method return `False`, as do negative integers. ::: ## Returns {.doc-returns} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [bool]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : `True` if the node exists, `False` otherwise. ::: ## Examples {.doc-examples} Both node IDs and labels work as lookups, and unknown identifiers return `False` rather than raising: ::: {#92a5d149 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} import edgecase as ec graph = ( ec.Graph() .add_node(label="Alice") .add_node(label="Bob") ) ( graph.has_node("Alice"), graph.has_node(1), graph.has_node("Charlie"), graph.has_node(999), ) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` (True, True, False, False) ``` ::: ::: A typical use is an "add if missing" pattern when loading records that may repeat a name. "Alice" already exists, so only "Carol" and "Dave" are added, giving four nodes: ::: {#92589cf2 .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} names = ["Alice", "Carol", "Alice", "Dave"] for name in names: if not graph.has_node(name): graph.add_node(label=name) graph.count_nodes() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=2} ``` 4 ``` ::: ::: Because strings are matched only against labels, the string `"1"` is not the same as node ID `1`: ::: {#8abc1456 .cell execution_count=3} ``` {.python .cell-code} graph.has_node(1), graph.has_node("1") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=3} ``` (True, False) ``` ::: :::
